lead: No source emits one pure wavelength: a DFB laser spans a fraction of a nanometre, an LED tens of nanometres. Each wavelength in a pulse travels at its own group velocity, so the pulse arrives stretched. This is chromatic (intramodal) dispersion, and it happens even in a single-mode fiber. The fiber is described by a dispersion coefficient D in ps/(nm·km); the spread it causes, Δτ, is a time in ps. D has two parts: a material part from the glass and a waveguide part from the guiding geometry.

blocks.text: Light energy travels at the group velocity v<sub>g</sub> = dω/dβ, where β is the propagation constant of the mode and ω the angular frequency. The group delay over a length L is τ = L/v<sub>g</sub>. Because τ changes with wavelength, two wavelengths Δλ apart arrive at different times. The dispersion coefficient is the change of group delay per kilometre per nanometre:

blocks.where: D is the dispersion coefficient in ps/(nm·km); τ is the group delay in ps; L is in km; λ is in nm.
Δτ is the pulse spread in ps; D in ps/(nm·km); L in km; Δλ is the spectral width of the source in nm.

blocks.text: This book takes D > 0 when the longer wavelengths arrive later (the “anomalous” region of standard fiber at 1550 nm). Some books use the opposite sign; fix one convention for a whole calculation. The two parts add with their signs:

blocks.where: D<sub>m</sub> is the material dispersion and D<sub>w</sub> the waveguide dispersion, both in ps/(nm·km).

blocks.text: The index of silica falls as wavelength rises, and the curve n(λ) bends. Material dispersion depends on that bend:

blocks.where: λ is the wavelength in m; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; d²n/dλ² is the curvature of the index curve in m⁻². The result is in s/m²; 1 s/m² = 10⁶ ps/(nm·km).

blocks.text: For pure silica D<sub>m</sub> crosses zero near 1270 nm; germania in the core moves this a little longer. Below the zero D<sub>m</sub> is negative, about −85 ps/(nm·km) at 850 nm, where the longer wavelengths arrive first. Above it D<sub>m</sub> is positive, about +21 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm. Some books write the material spread directly as σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>λ</sub>L/c)|λ d²n/dλ²|, where σ<sub>λ</sub> is the RMS spectral width; it is the same formula.

In a single-mode fiber part of the power travels in the cladding, and that share depends on the normalised frequency V = (2πa/λ)√(n₁² − n₂²), where a is the core radius. As λ rises, V falls, more of the mode spreads into the lower-index cladding, and its effective index moves from n₁ toward n₂. That change of β with wavelength, caused by geometry alone, is waveguide dispersion.

For a standard step-index single-mode fiber Dw is negative, about −4 ps/(nm·km) across 1300 to 1600 nm. Adding it to Dm pulls the zero of the total from about 1270 nm to about 1310 nm. Dw is the part a designer controls through a and Δ: a smaller core and a larger Δ make it more negative, which is how dispersion-shifted fibers move the zero to 1550 nm.
Near its zero λ₀ standard fiber is described by its zero-dispersion slope S₀, about 0.092 ps/(nm²·km):

blocks.where: D in ps/(nm·km); S₀ is the slope at λ₀ in ps/(nm²·km); λ and λ₀ in nm.

blocks.text: With λ₀ = 1310 nm this gives D = 17.5 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm, the familiar “about 17”. If a laser linewidth is given in frequency, convert it with Δλ = λ²Δf/c; at 1550 nm, 10 GHz is 0.080 nm. The bit-rate rule used in this book for a full spread is B ≤ 1/(2Δτ), as for intermodal dispersion.

examples.question: A 100 km single-mode link runs at 1550 nm with D = 17 ps/(nm·km). (a) Find the spread for a laser of spectral width 0.1 nm and the bit-rate limit B ≤ 1/(2Δτ). (b) Repeat for a 2 nm Fabry–Perot laser. (c) What does an LED of 40 nm width give?
steps: A twentyfold wider spectrum gives a twentyfold wider spread and a twentyfold lower limit.
examples.answer: 170 ps and 2.94 Gbit/s with the 0.1 nm laser; 3.4 ns and 147 Mbit/s with the 2 nm laser; 68 ns and 7.4 Mbit/s with the LED. Wide sources belong on short links.

examples.question: A standard fiber has λ₀ = 1310 nm and S₀ = 0.092 ps/(nm²·km). (a) Find D at 1550 nm. (b) A DFB laser at 1550 nm has a 20 GHz spectral width; convert it to nm and find the spread over 80 km.
examples.answer: D ≈ 17.5 ps/(nm·km); the 20 GHz line is 0.16 nm wide and spreads by about 224 ps over 80 km, more than two bit periods at 10 Gbit/s.

traps: Quoting the spread in ps/(nm·km). That is the unit of D; the spread Δτ = |D|LΔλ is a time in ps.
Putting a linewidth in GHz straight into Δτ = |D|LΔλ. Convert to nm first: 10 GHz at 1550 nm is only 0.08 nm.
Adding D<sub>m</sub> and D<sub>w</sub> as magnitudes. They have opposite signs above 1270 nm, and the partial cancellation is the point.
Saying the material zero is at 1310 nm. The glass alone has its zero near 1270 nm; 1310 nm is where D<sub>m</sub> + D<sub>w</sub> = 0.
Thinking a single-mode fiber has no dispersion. It has one mode but many wavelengths, so chromatic dispersion remains.

quiz.q: Define chromatic dispersion and give the unit of D.
quiz.a: Pulse spreading because the wavelengths in the source spectrum travel at different group velocities; D is in ps/(nm·km).

quiz.q: Which two parts add to give D?
quiz.a: Material dispersion D<sub>m</sub>, from the curvature of n(λ) of the glass, and waveguide dispersion D<sub>w</sub>, from the way the mode’s confinement changes with wavelength.

quiz.q: Why does an LED link suffer far more chromatic dispersion than a laser link with the same D and L?
quiz.a: Δτ is proportional to Δλ, and an LED is tens of nm wide against a fraction of a nm for a DFB laser.

quiz.q: An 80 km link at 1550 nm has D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and Δλ = 0.5 nm. Find Δτ and the limit B ≤ 1/(2Δτ).
Convert a 10 GHz linewidth at 1310 nm to nm.
Why is D<sub>w</sub> called the tunable part of chromatic dispersion?
quiz.a: D<sub>w</sub> depends on the core radius and Δ through V, which the preform design sets; D<sub>m</sub> is fixed by the glass composition and moves only a little with doping.

quiz.q: Standard fiber has D = 0 at 1310 nm, yet D<sub>m</sub> there is about +3.8 ps/(nm·km). Explain, using a material zero near 1270 nm.
quiz.a: D<sub>w</sub> ≈ −3.8 ps/(nm·km) at 1310 nm cancels it. The fiber’s zero is where D<sub>m</sub> = −D<sub>w</sub>, which lies about 40 nm above the material zero.

beyond: Coherent receivers now undo chromatic dispersion in digital signal processing, so a 400 Gbit/s channel crosses thousands of kilometres of standard fiber with no optical compensation. In short-reach links near 1310 nm (the O-band) dispersion stays small enough for simple direct detection. ITU-T G.652 specifies λ₀ between 1300 and 1324 nm and S₀ at most 0.092 ps/(nm²·km). Search for “G.652 dispersion formula”, “digital chromatic dispersion compensation” and “O-band data-centre links”.

figure.caption: Material dispersion of the glass crosses zero near 1270 nm; the negative waveguide part pulls the total zero to 1310 nm. At 1550 nm the parts are +21.0 and −3.5, giving D = 17.5 ps/(nm·km), the value of worked example 2.

spec.aria: Graph of dispersion against wavelength from 1200 to 1650 nanometres: a dashed material curve crossing zero at 1270, a dashed waveguide curve near minus 3.5, and the solid total crossing zero at 1310 and reaching 17.5 at 1550.
